en: Their long-haired giant.
If by chance he babbles nonsense,
Let us find a way.
If by chance he argues back,
Let us hack his breast apart.
Blustering and frightening them,
Let us get Akkelte.
If they hand over Kelte,
Let us part without ill words.
If they will not give Kelte,
Let us begin a grievous torment,
Let us cast our lives aside.
If they will not give Akkelte,
Let us begin a dreadful quarrel.
Double mail with lark-eye rings,
Let us turn it and put it on,
Let us exchange much gunfire,
Clashing ceaselessly for six months.”
Valiant Bakay spoke at length,
Speaking words that promised slaughter.
When the sun sank trembling,
When the first of the people lay down,
Pillowing their heads on white saddles,
With their heads toward Mecca,
They sank into a giant sleep,
And slept without stirring.
For Manas, whom Kydyr had blessed,
Valiant Bakay had been found.
For Manas, whom Baabedin had blessed,
Warrior Bakay had appeared.
His heart overflowing, set apart,
The rich man's son, hero Bakay,
In warrior Manas's eyes
Seemed a thousand vast armies.
When dawn grew pale,
When the first true dawn broke,
Leopard Bakay of princely blood
Woke with a start from sleep,
Turning over to his right.
‘Baabedin!’ he cried aloud.
Then Bakay once again
Called to Manas the lion:
‘Oh, my child, bloodthirsty Manas, leopard!
Did you see what I saw?
Did you perceive what I perceived?
Attend closely to my words:
A champion has come to you.
Now, if you will hear my words,
A hero has come to you.
The day clouded over; it was spring.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay
Was a man born beyond compare.
At enmity with his father,
Wearing a black robe of costly cloth,
Riding a horse like Kartküröng,
Towering in stature, broad in the shoulders,
Built like a warrior, broad in the chest,
Between unbelievers and Muslims
Your kinsman who will go as mediator,
Who will bring your sides together,
If you consider Azhybay,
He is your steed surpassing other men,
Who will serve you faithfully,
Your father's close kinsman.
Broad of jaw, broad of tongue,
A great orator who never errs,
Swift when he goes as mediator,
Knowing seventy kinds of speech,
Sharpening his dark tongue,
Pouring out words before the khan,
An eloquent, persuasive reasoner,
Today a great racer falls into your hands.
If you welcome him, he is the hero,
To your weary, solitary self,
He is the one to be a companion.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
He is the most resourceful of youths.
On a dark cliff no dog would tread,
He is the youth who will help you.
He will lend strength to your words.
If you welcome Azhybay,
He will bring you blessing.
Having walked among learned men,
Azhybay, the matchless orator,
Possesses learning too.
Sent into an assembly, he will not slip;
He has eloquence as well.
A champion in religion,
He is a spiritual master too.
Among all sorts of people,
When Azhybay arrives,
He is a religious scholar too.
Deft with a sudden turn of speech,
He has a pacer's smoothness too.
Stubbornly drinking millet beer,
Beating a holy man till he howls,
He does forbidden things as well.
He has a brazen nature too.
Among the wielders of the spear,
He is exceptionally nimble too.
He is the champion, he the support,
He is the hero who will mend your hurt.
God driving him, his allotted sustenance calling,
Know well, my lion, for you
This is the time he becomes a companion.
Never resting on the black mountain,
My khan Manas, listen:
Let him be the dark-mottled eagle.
Of wolf-maned Khan Azhybay,
Be the master who holds him.
Letting no bustard escape on the steppe,
Let him be the gray-mottled falcon.
Sending him out with a waving lure,
Be the master who tends him.
He is the valiant one and the support.
If you welcome Azhybay,
He is the hero to satisfy your desires.
Yesterday, in moon-dark springtime,
Quarreling with his father Argyn Khan,
He is the hero coming as a wanderer.
He is God's beloved servant.
If you welcome Azhybay,
He is the youth who will satisfy your longing.
That son of Argyn Khan,
Those who saw his bearing took fright.
He had studied wondrous lore.
Until he reached twenty-five,
He quietly pursued his studies.
Such was Azhybay's life;
He knew seventy kinds of speech.
When he reached twenty-six years,
He raised turmoil in the realm with a royal court,
And conquered the lower Kyzylbash people ten times.
Azhybay was exceedingly formidable,
His courage unlike any other's.
If you welcome Azhybay,
He is a renowned man worth the world.
His swift brown horse beneath him,
To all the people of the world was known
The havoc wrought by Azhybay.
The brown horse beneath him
Was sired by a stallion and born of a mare;
That dear creature of Father Kambar
Was born with everything in balance.
Left as a stallion, then gelded a horse,
When given his head and told ‘Go!’
He flew faster than a cloud.
His wondrous speed was beyond doubt;
Hearing a battle cry, he never panicked.
Among countless hosts of horses,
Once in front, he led them all.
He did not turn his neck like a common beast.
When he gave a single neigh,
The wild asses in the desert streamed along.
Hearing Kartküröng's voice,
No horsehair tail could stand still.
From among vast herds of horses,
He had raced up and joined them.
From the hollow of Chambyl-Bel,
Beside Kayyp-Bulak,
By God's decree he had appeared,
He had been found for Azhybay.
When he found Kartküröng,
The khan's son Azhybay
Thus found his honor sheltered.
When he put on his mountain-goatskin trousers,
The khan's son Azhybay,
When he mounted Kartküröng,
Besieged Khiva and took gold coins,
And took one dark-eyed girl.
Hardened by seeing thick battle dust,
He won the name of Azhybay.
Azhybay's nature had been revealed,
The tangles of his temper;
Then he had fallen into enmity,
Azhybay's father.
‘Since this Azhybay came forth,
All my countless livestock
He has squandered on wicked deeds,’ he said.
‘This boy Azhybay,
God the smiter has smitten him!’ he said.
When his father poured out his wrath,
‘Keep your livestock yourself,’ he said,
And left the livestock and departed.
With that, Argyn Khan
Disowned him as his son.
Azhybay was alone, the Turkmens many.
Barely escaping death,
That fellow, with his father,
Fought ceaselessly for six months,
Beginning a fierce wrath.
Countless riches, vast herds of livestock,
Offended with his father,
Azhybay, worn out,
Renounced them and abandoned them.
Without turning back, Azhybay
Attained his desire.
Turning away, he journeyed on,
Going far, not sparing his horse,
And entered Baghdad.
He pledged his hand to twelve spiritual guides,
Recited prayers with ten spiritual masters,
Went to the caliph and received a letter,
Received a blessing from the great spiritual master,
And made pilgrimage to a great holy place.
I hear of his renown: Azhybay
Has been named an illustrious champion.
My lion Manas, leopard,
Hear well what I say:
Make Azhybay your champion!
If you welcome Azhybay,
Sent scouting, he is your guide;
Going between parties, he is your envoy.
If you understand his temper, Azhybay
Is the flourishing market fortune gave you.
If loosed upon the shouting foe,
He will openly satisfy your longing.
Charging on his brown horse,
Answering back to his father,
Raging like a hungry lion,
Offended with his father,
The yellow gold that filled the treasury,
I heard he scattered as he left.
Offended with his father,
Seeking a mighty lion like you,
I heard he fled from home.
Finding no fertile sloping land,
I heard he left in resentment.
Finding no hero like you,
Finding no guarded, sloping ridge,
To join in struggles with,
Finding none as steadfast as you.
If you welcome Azhybay,
His words are sweet, his words are honey;
No such soul arises among men.
Never turning back from death,
He is the hero born keen and bold.
Never shrinking back from doom,
He is the lion born beyond compare.
He will grease your yurt's wall-felt with plenty.
If you encounter Azhybay,
He will make you khan on every side.
(An ocean among young men,
Your elder Bakay's equal.)
My child, at the earth's end, Zhelpinish,
I camped in a windy place.
Above all, Manas and Azhybay,
I longed for you both.
From travelers I heard word:
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
Wearing his horse down to the ribs,
Roaming the face of the earth,
I heard he sought a hero.
To satisfy his longing beyond measure,
I heard he sought a lion.
If we ride farther from here,
